book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

chapters.file: ch74 - 70. Jerry Seinfeld as Philosopher The Assimilated Sage of New Chelm.md
chapters.relation: Stern and Gimbel argue that Seinfeld's observational comedy is 'neo-Talmudic': like the rabbis who interpret the fixed text of the Torah, Seinfeld takes an accepted 'given' (shared phenomenological experience, e.g. the milk bit) and generates surprising wisdom by viewing it from an oblique angle. They read Seinfeld's outsider vantage through Du Bois's double consciousness (the assimilated Ashkenazi Jew who sees through two lenses at once) and invoke Derrida's differance as reintegrating Jewish pluralist epistemology into Western thought, with Nietzsche's slave-revolt as an analogy for how Jewish philosophy was made invisible. The sitcom Seinfeld, by contrast, is cast as the modern 'Chelm' joke cycle, parodying that same neo-Talmudic reasoning by pushing local logic (Elaine's Jujyfruits, Schindler's List) into absurdity.

chapters.file: ch75 - 71. Dave Chappelle as Philosopher Standing Up to Racism.md
chapters.relation: Benko and Burch treat Chappelle as a philosopher of race whose comedy of incongruity exposes the contradictions of American racism, reading his 'every Black American is bi-lingual' remark and sketches like 'Clayton Bigsby' and 'The Racial Draft' through Du Bois's double consciousness. They argue Chappelle's ethics of fairness, choice and personal responsibility unintentionally echoes Bonilla-Silva's 'color-blind racism,' and use bell hooks's Ain't I a Woman to show how his gendered 'Oppression Olympics' and use of 'bitch' reproduce the sexism hooks says Black men absorb, so his trans and gender jokes rank Black men as the most oppressed group. The chapter's core apparatus (incongruity/schema theory of humor, color-blind racism) sits outside the taxonomy.

chapters.file: ch76 - 72. Ricky Gervais as Philosopher The Comedy of Alienation.md
chapters.relation: Gardner argues that Gervais's series are not merely 'cringe comedy' but a 'comedy of alienation' dramatizing Marx's four aspects of estrangement under capitalism. The Office illustrates alienation from the product of labor (Wernham Hogg workers reduced to sales figures, Tim's crushed inner life); Extras shows alienation from the activity of labor (background artists treated as props, Maggie humiliated by Clive Owen); The Office/Extras/After Life show alienation from species-being and from others (Brent's 'anyone of them will do'); and Derek depicts a character who transcends alienation. She reads The Invention of Lying through Marx's 'religion is the opium of the people,' showing belief in an afterlife pacifies workers without changing an exploitative, commodifying society.

chapters.file: ch77 - 73. Hasan Minhaj as Philosopher Navigating the Struggles of Identity.md
chapters.relation: Singh reads Minhaj's comedy of identity through existentialism, arguing his call for 'authenticity' over the first generation's 'assimilation' (the 'American dream tax' and 'biryani' arguments about choosing one's life) enacts Sartre's existence-precedes-essence and rejection of bad faith. He frames Minhaj's Indian-American-Muslim conflict via Heidegger's thrownness and facticity and the move from the they-self (das Man) to authentic self, contrasting it with Sartre's facticity as a limit on freedom. Minhaj's 'global citizen' anti-nationalism, his 'love is bigger than fear,' and 'may the best argument win' are presented as prescriptions for navigating national, ethnic, religious and personal identity while flagging fallacies like hasty generalization behind Islamophobia.

chapters.file: ch78 - 74. Stephen Fry as Philosopher The Manic Socrates.md
chapters.relation: Innes casts Fry as a 'manic Socrates,' a satirical gadfly whose Horatian, Juvenalian and Menippean satire (Bit of Fry and Laurie sketches, the Gay Byrne 'bone cancer in children' God interview, the Intelligence Squared debate) mocks the military, social class and the Church to provoke the Socratic examined life. Fry's attack on theodicy is read through Plato's Euthyphro dilemma and the problem of evil, and his flight to Belgium and relationship with the 'luvvies' through Sartre's No Exit, the Look, and bad faith. Using Bourdieu's habitus, Innes concludes Fry 'praises the institutions with faint mockery,' seeking only moderate reform he can afford as a guest of the upper class rather than Socratic radical change.

chapters.file: ch79 - 75. Phoebe Waller-Bridge as Philosopher Conscious Women Making Choices.md
chapters.relation: Pande and Engels argue that Fleabag and Lulu (Crashing) embody Sartrean authenticity: they own their choices, balance facticity and transcendence, and stay outside bad faith, while the men (Anthony, the Priest) fall back on pregiven roles and let 'the Look' or their fundamental project decide for them. Fleabag's addressing the camera and finally shutting it out is read as breaking the gaze of the Other; the Priest choosing priesthood over love exemplifies denial of transcendence. Through Beauvoir's Second Sex, woman-as-Other, and ethics of ambiguity, they show Waller-Bridge's transgressive, sexually frank women reclaim self-definition, arguing viewers 'could do better to be' the kind of free, choosing women her protagonists are.

chapters.file: ch81 - 76. The Last of Us as Moral Philosophy Teleological Particularism and Why Joel Is Not a Villain.md
chapters.relation: Horn takes The Last of Us as moral philosophy, arguing Joel is read as a villain only because players assume consequentialism or deontology. On Bentham/Mill's utilitarianism Joel fails to maximize utility by killing many to save Ellie; on Kant's categorical imperative his lying, stealing and killing are always impermissible. Horn instead defends 'teleological particularism' — an agent acts rightly when acting in conformity with a role, roles being socially constructed and variable — so Joel's role as Ellie's surrogate father (mirrored in his carrying her out as he carried Sarah, and the 'Future Days' lyric) obligates him to put her above humanity. On this view Joel's refusal to let the Fireflies kill Ellie, and his final lie, are morally permissible, not villainous.

chapters.file: ch82 - 77. Journey as Philosophy Meaning, Connection, and the Sublime.md
chapters.relation: Hamer argues Journey works through the interplay of connection, the sublime and meaning. The wordless multiplayer bond with an unnameable stranger before vast vistas dramatizes emotional connection where the ancestors' greed failed. The looming mountain and immense dunes evoke the sublime, read through Burke's pleasurable terror and Kant's mathematical and dynamical sublime (imagination overwhelmed while reason comprehends; feeling power over a nature that cannot harm the deathless player, then rebirth surpassing the sublime into joy). The cyclical return to the start recasts the game as Camus's Myth of Sisyphus: a meaningless repeated ascent that players nonetheless replay, so we must imagine the Traveler — and ourselves — happy to make the beautiful repetition our own.

chapters.file: ch83 - 78. The Witness as Philosophy How Knowledge Is Constructed.md
chapters.relation: Cuddy asks what epistemology Blow built into The Witness's frustrating puzzles and its windmill videos (Burke, Feynman, Moriarty, Spira, Gangaji). He rejects the sophistic/Protagorean 'knowledge depends on the observer' reading (most puzzles have objective, inductive-and-deductive solutions, e.g. the yellow-glass bunker) and the strict scientific realism of the Burke video defended by Putnam's no-miracles argument. Using Plato's cave and the aporia of Socrates' Meno (the puzzle's 'ah-ha' epiphanies), and Kuhn's incommensurable paradigm shifts (the game's 'hard left turns' forcing players to overhaul their understanding), he concludes the game argues that true knowledge is attainable, individually and collectively, though reached by a nonlinear, paradigm-shifting route rather than pure realism or relativism.

chapters.file: ch84 - 79. Cyberpunk 2077 as Philosophy Balancing the (Mystical) Ghost in the (Transhuman) Machine.md
chapters.relation: Lay reads Cyberpunk 2077's transhuman Night City against the enhancement debate. Using the Ship of Theseus, Parfit's continuity plus fission/fusion (V and Johnny 'fusing,' the Delamain AIs) and Clark and Chalmers's extended mind, he argues enhancement neither destroys personal identity (which Parfit says doesn't matter) nor dehumanizes users — it may be the purest expression of Clark's cyborg humanity. The real danger is corporate exploitation of bodies, explained via Adorno's culture industry and Arendt's banality of evil. Buddhist nonattachment (Nagarjuna's emptiness, echoed by a Schopenhauer shard) grounds each ending's pacification-versus-attachment theme, but Lay corrects it with Weil's critique of power and Buber's I-Thou, concluding the game urges transcending the boundary between 'me' and 'you' through mystical interpersonal relation.

holes.name: Talmudic / Jewish Pluralist Epistemology
holes.what: A Jewish mode of knowing that accepts fixed commands (mitzvot) that are neither true nor false and generates wisdom through a multiplicity of contextual interpretations, dialogic rather than the unitary Hellenic-Christian search for one truth.
holes.why: Chapter 74's entire thesis is that Seinfeld's 'neo-Talmudic' comedy instantiates this distinctively Jewish epistemology, which no existing philosopher or concept slug in the taxonomy captures.

holes.name: Philosophy of Humor
holes.what: The philosophical study of what jokes are and how comedy generates insight, e.g. incongruity and superiority theories of laughter.
holes.why: Chapters 74-79 all treat comedians as philosophers and lean on theories of how humor (incongruity, schema-shifting) produces wisdom, a recurring load-bearing topic the taxonomy lacks a slug for.

holes.name: Color-Blind Racism
holes.what: Post-1960s racism (Bonilla-Silva) that minimizes systemic racism while stressing individual choice and responsibility, sustaining a 'white habitus' through coded cultural, not biological, explanations of inequality.
holes.why: Chapter 75 argues Chappelle's ethics of fairness and personal responsibility overlaps with color-blind racism, the analytic frame of the whole chapter, which has no taxonomy slug.

holes.name: Habitus and Social Capital
holes.what: Bourdieu's account of the ingrained dispositions, tastes and social capital by which individuals reproduce and maintain their social class membership.
holes.why: Chapter 78 uses Bourdieu's habitus (and his Blackadder analysis) as the mechanism explaining why Fry's 'faint mockery' reinforces the class and institutions he mocks; neither Bourdieu nor habitus is in the taxonomy.

holes.name: Role Ethics (Teleological Particularism)
holes.what: The view that at least some moral obligations derive from the socially constructed roles an agent occupies (father, doctor, citizen), and that these role-based duties are relative to subject, time and culture rather than universal.
holes.why: Chapter 81's central thesis is the author's own 'teleological particularism,' a role-based ethics distinct from consequentialism, deontology, and moral particularism, for which the taxonomy offers no adequate slug.

holes.name: The Sublime
holes.what: The aesthetic experience of pleasurable terror or awe before the vast, powerful or infinite, distinguished from beauty; developed by Burke (pain-based terror at a distance) and Kant (mathematical and dynamical sublime).
holes.why: Chapter 82 builds its analysis of Journey on the sublime as a category separate from beauty, drawing centrally on Burke, whom the taxonomy lacks, and on a sense of the sublime broader than the existing kant-aesthetics slug.

holes.name: Transhumanism and Posthumanism
holes.what: The project (and debate over) using technology and enhancement to transcend normal biological limits of human body and mind, up to a posthuman state, weighing benefits against threats to identity, autonomy and human dignity.
holes.why: Chapter 84's whole subject is transhuman enhancement in Cyberpunk 2077 and the enhancement debate (Bostrom, Huxley, Kurzweil, Agar), a topic with no dedicated concept slug in the taxonomy.

holes.name: Simone Weil
holes.what: A French philosopher and Christian mystic (1909-1943) who analyzed power/force as a mutually damaging social relation and proposed universal obligations of compassion to meet the 'needs of the soul.'
holes.why: Chapter 84 uses Weil's critique of power and her mysticism of interpersonal obligation as one of the two thinkers grounding its final answer to transhuman corporatism, but Weil is absent from the taxonomy.
